summary: Extends RSVP so some sessions can be given priority when the network is congested and there is not room for everyone. That raises the chance that important sessions, such as emergency or government calls, can still be set up. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When a theme park is full, some guests with a special pass still get in. This lets certain network connections get a special pass when the network is crowded.

questions: how to prioritize sessions during congestion

difference between admission priority and preemption priority

subtitle: How RSVP can tag some reservations as higher priority so important sessions still get bandwidth when the network is crowded.

tldr.problem: Some sessions need a better chance of being set up when the network is congested, but RSVP had no way to say that a reservation deserves preferred access to bandwidth without preempting others.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6401 defines two RSVP policy elements: an Application-Level Resource Priority element that carries the application's priority, and a small Admission Priority element that routers use to pick which bandwidth limits apply to a reservation.
tldr.outcome: Routers can admit priority reservations that would otherwise be refused, without preempting existing sessions. The extensions are intended for use within a single administrative domain.

today: RFC 6401 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text says the extensions are intended for use within a single administrative domain, not end-to-end on the Internet.

sections.title: The Problem: Priority Under Congestion
sections.content:
Some applications need an elevated probability of session establishment for specific sessions when the network is congested. Part of the answer can sit at the session layer, for example a SIP system that queues or bumps less important session requests. Part can sit at the network layer, through admission control that gives prioritized access to resources such as bandwidth.

Networks normally have engineered capacity limits for a class of traffic. Admission priority can set aside some bandwidth out of those limits for prioritized sessions only. Alternatively, it can let prioritized sessions take extra resources beyond the limits applied to normal sessions. RFC 6401 provides the RSVP extensions to signal this.

It differs from RFC 3181, whose Signaled Preemption Priority Policy Element lets a node preempt already admitted sessions. Here the goal is to raise the chance of establishment without preempting existing sessions. A reservation may carry admission priority, preemption priority, or both.
sections.eli5: When the network is nearly full, some important calls should still get through. This document gives those calls a way to say how important they are, without kicking anyone else off.

sections.title: How the Two Policy Elements Work Together
sections.content:
The design splits the job in two. The new Application-Level Resource Priority (ALRP) policy element carries the application's own priority requirement. For SIP, the end devices simply copy the value of the Resource-Priority header from RFC 4412 into it.

At the edge of a policy area, the policy decision points (PDPs) read the ALRP element and map it to an admission priority level for that area. They convey it in the new Admission Priority policy element. Downstream RSVP routers, which have a local policy decision point but no controlling PDP, can then enforce the priority at every hop, even hops that know nothing about application-level priority.

The RFC says the ALRP element is not expected to be used at hops inside a policy area. It is used at the boundaries to set or reset the Admission Priority element. The same mapping can feed the preemption priority of RFC 3181 when preemption is wanted, and it can also be used at boundaries with other signaling protocols such as NSLP.
sections.eli5: The ticket you show at the park gate says what kind of guest you are. The gate staff then give you a simple colored wristband, and every ride just checks the wristband.

sections.title: The Admission Priority Policy Element
sections.content:
The Admission Priority element is deliberately simple, stateless and lightweight, so a node's local policy decision point can process it and its enforcement point can apply it. It is 12 bytes long: the Length field is always 12, and the P-Type is ADMISSION_PRI with value 0x05.

The one field that matters is Adm. Priority, an 8-bit unsigned value where higher values mean higher priority. It effectively says which bandwidth constraints of the bandwidth model in use apply to admitting this reservation. The Flags and Reserved fields MUST be set to zero on transmit and ignored on reception.

The Merge Strategy and Error Code fields apply to multicast flows. Merge rules come from an IANA registry shared with RFC 3181. RFC 6401 does not recommend a merge strategy for admission priority, and notes that "take highest priority" means taking the highest numerical value.

This element does not say the reservation may preempt anything. A session that needs both must carry both an Admission Priority and a Preemption Priority element, which are handled as separate mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The wristband is a tiny label with one number on it. A bigger number means more important. Having the wristband does not let you push anyone out of line.

sections.title: The Application-Level Resource Priority Element
sections.content:
The ALRP element has a Length (in octets, which MUST be a multiple of 4), a P-Type of APP_RESOURCE_PRI with value 0x06, and then a list of ALRPs. Each ALRP holds a 16-bit ALRP Namespace, 8 reserved bits and an 8-bit ALRP Value.

The namespace and value numbers come from IANA registries for SIP Resource-Priority namespaces and priority values, which this RFC extended with numerical values.

When POLICY_DATA objects are integrity protected, local policy decision points should not modify them and MUST forward them unchanged. For multicast, when they are not protected, a node MAY merge incoming ALRP elements. The outgoing list MUST be the union of the incoming lists, and a given ALRP MUST NOT appear more than once.

Policy Ignorant Nodes and policy-capable nodes that do not recognize these elements pass them along using the default handling of RFC 2750.
sections.eli5: The ticket is a short list of notes saying which kind of pass you hold and how high it ranks. If lots of tickets travel together, the list can be combined, but no note is written twice.

sections.title: Bandwidth Allocation Models
sections.content:
The RFC does not mandate how routers turn an admission priority into a decision. Models from Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering may be reused: the Maximum Allocation Model (RFC 4125), the Russian Dolls Model (RFC 4127) and Maximum Allocation with Reservation (RFC 4126). Appendix A illustrates them and adds a Priority Bypass Model (PrBM). These are informative and not a recommended course of action.

With the Maximum Allocation Model, priority traffic cannot use more than the bandwidth made available to it, even if non-priority traffic is not using all of its own.

With the PrBM, non-priority sessions are subject to bandwidth admission control. A priority session is admitted regardless of the current load, so it is never rejected. The RFC's rationale is that priority sessions are very rare most of the time and are a small share of load even in congestion, so they are unlikely to cause noticeable QoS degradation.
sections.eli5: The park can reserve some seats just for pass holders, or it can let pass holders walk straight in even when the line is closed to everyone else. This document does not pick one.

sections.title: Security and Where to Use It
sections.content:
Some RSVP messages use the Router Alert Option, and given the concerns discussed in RFC 6398, the extensions are intended for use within a single administrative domain. They are not meant for end-to-end use on the Internet. The RFC suggests that a network can protect itself against leaked RSVP by not enabling RSVP, or at its edge by tunneling or, as a last resort, dropping incoming RSVP messages.

The policy elements travel inside a POLICY_DATA object, so their integrity can be protected in two optional ways. RSVP authentication between neighbors SHOULD be supported, using shared keys to sign messages. An INTEGRITY object inside the POLICY_DATA object MAY be supported, which helps when some nodes are Policy Ignorant Nodes.
sections.eli5: The special pass only makes sense inside one park. The park can also put a seal on the pass so that nobody can quietly change it on the way.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA allocated two RSVP policy element P-Types: 0x05 for ADMISSION_PRI and 0x06 for APP_RESOURCE_PRI.

A Merge Strategy registry now applies to both this element and the Preemption Priority element. It lists value 0 as Reserved, 1 as take priority of highest QoS, 2 as take highest priority and 3 as force error on heterogeneous merge. A new Error Code registry lists 0 as NO_ERROR and 2 as HETEROGENEOUS, with 1 reserved for consistency with RFC 3181.

IANA also extended the SIP Resource-Priority Namespaces and Priority-Values registries with numerical values. Within a namespace values are allocated in decreasing order ending with 0, so the greatest priority gets value 0.
sections.eli5: A librarian wrote the new codes in the official book so everyone uses the same numbers for the same things.
